We subsequently discuss how we have since optimized nanopath's evaluation suite to be an even more faithful, quick proxy for external benchmarking. Nanopath provides an accessible testbed for students, researchers, and AI agents to explore pathology foundation modeling through fair, transparent, and directly comparable experiments.

title: The Truth Beneath the Tokens: Prompt-Space Recovery of Knowledge Edits in Language Models
summary: Model editing provides an efficient way to update factual knowledge in transformer models. Recent approaches reverse edits by modifying, masking, or decomposing model weights, but make recovery dependent on weight-space interventions. We instead show that pre-edit knowledge can be recovered through input-space interventions alone, without modifying the edited model's weights. We introduce Memento, a prompt-space mechanism for auditing residual knowledge that learns a reusable recovery signal to steer an edited model toward its pre-edit response. Memento supports both continuous recovery prefixes and discrete textual prompts for standard text interfaces. Across three LLMs and five editing techniques, Memento recovers 80.07% of held-out edited facts, achieving a 9.58% relative improvement over baselines, suggesting that editing may suppress the facts without fully eliminating their recoverability. We further investigate whether prompt-space recovery extends beyond model editing. On pristine, unedited LLMs, Memento improves average factual recall by 53.9% relative to standard inference. These results demonstrate the potential of prompt-space recovery for auditing residual knowledge in edited models and investigating the gap between factual knowledge and its accessibility during inference. We will release our source code.

title: Beyond Hash Matching: AI-Based Detection of Previously Unidentified CSAM and its Legal Implications in the EU
summary: The detection of previously unidentified Child Sexual Abuse Material (CSAM) remains a significant challenge for law enforcement authorities, online service providers, and child protection organizations, as traditional hash-matching technologies are primarily designed to identify previously verified material. This paper reviews and classifies existing AI-based technologies that could complement hash-based approaches and support the detection, analysis, and prioritization of potentially harmful content. The reviewed approaches are organized into three categories: real-time image and video analysis, image and video classification and tagging, and AI-based behavioral monitoring. A comparative analysis examines the capabilities, limitations, and potential integration of general-purpose computer vision platforms, content moderation services, and specialized CSAM detection tools within existing detection workflows. An experimental evaluation was conducted using Google Cloud Vision AI and Sightengine to investigate sexual-content classification and child-adult age estimation. The results highlight differences in classification taxonomies and outputs across providers, as well as significant limitations in age classification, particularly for adolescents. These findings highlight the importance of using AI-based assessments as complementary tools for analysis and prioritization, rather than as definitive determination of CSAM. Finally, the paper examines the relevant European Union regulatory framework, with particular attention to the EU AI Act, the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR), fundamental rights, transparency, accountability, and human oversight. The legal analysis highlights how regulatory obligations and safeguards may differ depending on the deployment context, potentially creating inconsistencies across interconnected detection and reporting workflows.

title: LongCapHarness: Capability-Guided Auto-Harnessing for Long-Context Reasoning
summary: Existing methods enhancing an LLM's long-context reasoning capability often rely on data synthesis and follow-up LLM post-training. However, the data synthesis strategy and the post-training recipes are empirically driven and computationally intensive. In this work, we propose a new framework, dubbed LongCapHarness, to instead harness the underlying capabilities for long-context reasoning. The harnessing process recursively revises and updates capability primitive implementation, capability state and control logic through recursive self-improvement on the development set. With neither data synthesis nor LLM post-training, LongCapHarness is applied to Llama3-8B and transferred to Qwen2.5-3B. LongCapHarness substantially outperforms recent data-synthesis-based baselines on HELMET and RULER benchmarks; its estimated development cost is less than 50% of the estimated training costs of NExtLong and PolicyLong. We hope these results motivate further research into harnessing the latent capabilities of LLMs to solve tasks beyond their explicit training.

title: GMD-Mamba: Lightweight 3D Medical Image Segmentation Using a Grouped Multi-Directional Mamba
comment: It is a four pages paper with 2 figures and submitted to ISBI2027
summary: Mamba has the capability to capture global context in linear time for 3D medical image segmentation. However, existing methods employ Mamba with full-width directional scans at every resolution, keeping the model large (64-138M parameters and high FLOPs). We propose Grouped Multi-Directional (GMD) Mamba, a lightweight network based on the GMD scan that divides input channels $C$ into groups $G$ and flattens each group in different directions in one pass. This gives multi-directional context at $O(C^2/G)$ instead of $O(K \cdot C^2)$, where $K$ is the number of scan directions. Additionally, we employ Mamba only at the deepest encoder stages, resulting in 19.2M parameters. On BraTS2023, it achieves the best average Dice of 92.0% and the lowest HD95 of 2.7 at $\sim$1/7 the parameters of SegMamba-V2. For model validation, we also ran experiments on the MSD Spleen dataset, achieving competitive performance. The implementation details and code are publicly available at https://github.com/2802990u/GMD-Mamba.

title: Hibana: Fast Agentic Inference on Unified-Memory Devices
summary: Local AI promises capable personal assistants that run on users' own devices, keeping data and computation under their control. Open-weight models that fit on local devices can now handle practical tasks such as coding. Yet current inference engines fall short. Popular engines such as vLLM and SGLang target datacenter GPUs with dedicated host memory, while local engines underuse the memory hierarchy of unified-memory devices. We present Hibana, an inference engine for unified-memory devices that co-optimizes model representation, memory management, and decoding strategy. Model surgery, the process of editing a trained model's architecture to suit its hardware, changes how the model computes, shrinking its memory footprint and data movement. Unified-memory management preserves each agent's state across turns, so long-running agents can resume instantly instead of recomputing their state. Adaptive speculation generates several tokens per step. Hibana codesigns these features around the shared memory capacity and limited bandwidth of unified-memory systems-on-chip to support local multi-agent workloads. On a single DGX Spark serving Qwen and Nemotron models of up to 125B parameters, Hibana completes up to 3.4$\times$ more agentic tasks per hour and delivers up to 3.9$\times$ higher decoding throughput than other established frameworks such as vLLM, NVIDIA Flare, llama.cpp, and TensorFold. Code is available at https://github.com/sharar-project/hibana.

title: Ultra-Lightweight 3D Medical Image Segmentation via Knowledge Distillation in Label-Scarce Domains
comment: This is a four pages paper having 3 figures and is submitted to ISBI2027
summary: Mamba is a neural network architecture that reduces computational complexity, and has been shown to be effective for 3D medical image segmentation. However, existing models still remain computationally expensive. We propose compressing Mamba by distillation while achieving competitive performance. Specifically, we demonstrate compression of a 139M-parameter SegMamba-V2 teacher into a lightweight TinyUNet3D student with about 0.96M parameters, achieving about 145$\times$ compression with a performance drop of just over one Dice point. We further investigate the utility of knowledge distillation in a range of data-labeling scenarios under identical experimental settings, and show that its advantage is most prominent when labeled data is scarce. To demonstrate the generalizability of our approach, experiments are conducted on three datasets: BraTS 2023, MSD Spleen and MSD Hippocampus. The code for TinyUNet3D is publicly available at: https://github.com/2802990u/tinyunet3d-dist-kd.

title: Test-Time Scaling for Diffusion Language Models with Frequency-Aware Remasking
summary: Diffusion language models (DLMs) generate text through iterative denoising, where decisions about which tokens to commit or remask strongly affect output quality. Existing certainty-aware strategies rely on instantaneous confidence or entropy, but these local signals can be misleading on difficult reasoning problems. We formulate DLM test-time scaling as adaptive allocation of both inference compute and decoding strategies. Our two-stage approach uses a fast base sampler to solve easy questions, then applies frequency-aware remasking to the remaining hard questions. This strategy tracks how often each token's prediction changes across denoising steps and preferentially commits frequently changing tokens, encouraging samples to explore alternative reasoning paths rather than collapse onto the model's preferred trajectory. Experiments with LLaDA-8B-Instruct and Dream-7B-Instruct show consistent improvements over a strong adaptive allocation baseline, with absolute accuracy gains of up to 3.73 percentage points (LLaDA) and 7.33 percentage points (Dream) on MATH-500, and absolute coverage gains of up to 11.39 percentage points (LLaDA) and 10.98 percentage points (Dream) on HumanEval. On questions unsolved by the base certainty-aware strategy after 100 samples, frequency-aware remasking recovers solutions for 3.75% to 18.75% of examples.

title: REFORM-3D: A Representation-Centric Evaluation Framework for 3D Medical Vision Foundation Models
comment: 32 pages, 6 figures, Accepted to NeurIPS 2026 ED Track
summary: Evaluation of 3D medical foundation models is typically dominated by downstream task scores, which entangle representation quality with adaptation choices. This is especially critical in volumetric imaging, where spacing and anisotropy can substantially alter image statistics while the anatomy itself remains unchanged. We therefore introduce \textbf{REFORM-3D}, a \textbf{R}epresentation-centric \textbf{E}valuation \textbf{F}ramew\textbf{OR}k for benchmarking frozen 3D medical vision foundation \textbf{M}odels across three questions: Acquisition Robustness, asking whether features remain stable when spacing varies while anatomy is fixed; Cross-Modal Anatomical Alignment, asking whether labeled anatomical structures remain recoverable across modalities under balanced bidirectional retrieval; and Anatomical Transfer, asking whether organ identity remains recoverable from limited labeled support under case-disjoint evaluation. These are also pretraining questions, because what a 3D encoder learns depends on how volumes are geometrically presented during self-supervised pretraining. We further introduce Med3DINO encoder family, pretrained on $62.6$K unlabeled MR, CT, PET, CTA, and CBCT volumes under three explicit geometric assumptions: isotropic normalization, voxel-relative sampling, and spacing-aware resampling. Across Med3DINO and heterogeneous external encoders, REFORM-3D reveals module-specific strengths rather than a single model ordering. Within the controlled Med3DINO comparison, voxel-relative sampling yields lower embedding drift, whereas spacing-aware resampling favors anatomical transfer; semantic-transfer advantages depend on the dataset and feature type. Project link: \href{https://endarzboy.github.io/reform3d-website/}{\highlightLR{REFORM-3D}}.

title: Distinguishing Extraction Failures and Clinical Discordance with LLM Uncertainty on Radiology Reports
comment: Accepted as a spotlight presentation at ML4H 2026, published at Proceedings of Machine Learning Research 346
summary: Large language models (LLMs) can structure clinical datasets, but extraction error must be distinguished from discordance in the underlying data. From a real-world cohort of 1{,}045 patients undergoing coronary CT angiography (CCTA), we evaluated whether LLM uncertainty during vessel-level coronary artery disease (CAD) stenosis extraction could identify extraction failure and clinical discordance. References were expert CCTA annotations (253 patients) and subsequent invasive coronary angiography (ICA; 729 patients). We quantify extraction failure as disagreement between stenosis severity in LLM extracted versus expert annotations, and clinical discordance as disagreement in stenosis severity between CCTA and subsequent ICA. Stenosis Margin, selected from ten candidate measures, was used to quantify LLM uncertainty, and generalized estimating equation logistic regression and AUC evaluated its association and incremental discrimination for each failure mode. LLM uncertainty was strongly associated with extraction failure (adjusted OR 4.15 [95% CI 2.57--6.69], $P<0.001$) and substantially improved discrimination beyond LLM-extracted CCTA stenosis severity alone (AUC 0.81 to 0.86; $Δ$AUC $+0.06$ [$+0.03$, $+0.09$], $P=0.001$). In contrast, LLM uncertainty weakly associated with clinical discordance (adjusted OR 1.22 [1.04--1.43], Holm-adjusted $P=0.118$) but provided no incremental discrimination beyond LLM-extracted CCTA stenosis severity ($Δ$AUC $+0.01$ [$-0.00$, $+0.02$], $P=0.245$). Moreover, extraction errors and clinical discordance showed little overlap, with 38 of 42 clinically discordant vessels (90%) having been extracted correctly. LLM uncertainty may identify extraction failures without identifying underlying clinical discordance, supporting failure attribution when evaluating LLM-derived clinical datasets.

title: VLM as an Editing Pilot: VLM-Steered Velocity Control for Flow-Based Image Editing
summary: Text-guided image editing requires realizing the requested semantic change while preserving content unrelated to the instruction. FlowEdit provides an efficient inversion-free solution, but its source-anchored coupling can become overly restrictive, causing zero-edit, where the output remains close to the source and the requested change fails to emerge. We find that source coupling directly governs the preservation--editing trade-off, while a fixed coupling schedule cannot adapt to timestep-specific editing needs. Motivated by this observation, we propose V2C-Edit, a training-free VLM-steered velocity control framework. V2C-Edit constructs complementary coupling-controlled velocities and dynamically selects among them using Instruction-Level Similarity (ILS), which evaluates whether the predicted transformation follows the editing instruction. Adaptive spatial masking further preserves regions unrelated to the edit. Experiments on MagicBrush and PIE-Bench with FLUX and Stable Diffusion 3 show that V2C-Edit consistently improves instruction alignment over FlowEdit while maintaining competitive structural preservation, and that ILS better reflects editing effectiveness than target-caption CLIP similarity. Our code is available at https://github.com/Kuanshen77/V2C-Edit.

title: Imperfectly Imperfect: Evaluating Graded Cognitive Diversity in LLM Persona Simulations
comment: Accepted at NeurIPS 2026 (Evaluations & Datasets Track). 42 pages, 14 figures. Code: https://github.com/sion-w/CogSuite
summary: Large language model (LLM) agents are increasingly used as synthetic participants in social, behavioural, and decision-making research, yet it remains unclear whether they can express graded cognitive diversity as assigned when engaging in simulated behaviour. We introduce a cognition-suite evaluation that tests whether simulated populations reproduce human variation in reasoning, self-reported traits, their associations, and downstream behaviour. Agents conditioned on synthetic or human-derived profiles of cognitive reflection, Need for Cognition, and Big Five personality answer the same suite as a cohort of 473 adults: two newly assembled tests, a Cognitive Reflection Test (CRT) and a Behavioural Reflection Test (BRT) whose decision scenarios measure reflection in behaviour, alongside an established CRT and the two trait questionnaires. Across seven full-battery simulation runs of four models, agents recover Need for Cognition and Big Five trait distributions on self-report questionnaires, but fall short on simulating diversity of cognitive task performance and downstream behaviours. In the four Claude Sonnet 4.6 runs, every agent scores full marks on both CRTs, whatever reflection level its persona was assigned. In the other three runs agents make intuitive-lure errors (the tempting wrong answers CRT items invite), but 49 to 85% score full marks, against under 10% in the human sample. Claude Sonnet 5 comes closest to people's item-by-item pattern of lures; the other two runs give fewer lures and vary less between items. In the BRT scenarios, every run over-produces 8 to 11 of 15 coded behaviours by at least 20 percentage points, and people's links between reflection and behaviour carry over only in part. Useful synthetic populations must preserve not only trait descriptors but the structured variation in reasoning, error type, and behaviour those descriptors are meant to organise.

title: Same Pixels, Different Documents: Measuring Part-Level Editability in Image Vectorization
summary: Image vectorization is often evaluated by rendering fidelity, which cannot distinguish documents that render identically but support different edits. Edit-based evaluation tests outcomes, but an oracle that gathers a part's fragments can conceal the cost of selecting them. We introduce Pass@k, which tests whether a prescribed edit can succeed using objects selectable within k clicks under a specified interaction model. Eight document diagnostics characterize properties relevant to editing beyond these tasks. We assess structural sensitivity through controlled perturbations, practical relevance through designer operations, and reference dependence through alternative drawings. We evaluate twelve open and commercial methods on 211 references, with 635 edit tasks on 93 of them. In each of four reference sets, including two drawn by designers, 64-88% of oracle-passed tasks on parts composed of multiple shapes fail at Pass@1, against 6-40% for single shapes, pooling counts over configurations. Higher fidelity does not guarantee higher Pass@1, while selected diagnostics are associated with designers' effort in our study.

title: AFVE-Bench: Measuring Abandoned-Frame Verbalization Errors in Multi-Turn LLM Revision
summary: Multi-turn revision often asks a model to replace an earlier organizing frame while preserving still-valid facts and artifact requirements. Existing instruction-following evaluations mainly assess the latest target and may therefore score an artifact as successful even when it adopts the new frame but exposes the superseded one. We call this failure an abandoned-frame verbalization error (AFVE). AFVE-Bench evaluates silent frame replacement in English and Chinese using 192 matched four-turn dialogues across eight writing domains. Each seed has zero, one, or two pre-target user requests to generate under the source frame. AFVE eligibility depends on the user-request history and applies to the one- and two-request conditions; the zero-request condition serves as a frame-bearing baseline. Eleven model configurations yielded 4,224 expected post-target response units. Two annotators independently scored 4,204 scorable responses for target adoption, source-frame verbalization, and direct usability; model and condition metadata were hidden, and disagreements were adjudicated. AFVE occurs in 25.54% (715/2,799) of history-conditioned responses. Of 2,388 target-passing history-conditioned responses, 472 (19.77%) still expose the abandoned source frame, most often through contrastive framing (423/472). For these standalone revision tasks, target adoption does not ensure source-frame silence.

title: Adapting Frozen Promptable Segmenters to User-Defined Taxonomies via Few-Shot Proposal Learning
summary: Promptable segmenters of the SAM family turn a click or a phrase into an instance mask, so the costly part of a label is now its class. However, each annotation project draws its own class boundary, often through objects these models already know: people from cars, sedans from trucks, one sedan model from another. A generic model's boundary is fixed by its training vocabulary. We present SNAP, an annotation pipeline that learns the project's boundary from the labels the annotator draws anyway. On one frozen SAM2.1 pass per image, we fit a per-project head, SnapHead, that classifies every proposal and refits in seconds after each labeled image. Where SAM 3 is available, the same labels decide class by class whether to keep its boundary or ours. Given the true masks of eight look-alike cell lines, SAM 3 assigns classes at Cohen's kappa = 0.038 and SnapHead at 0.754 (60 labeled images), and when only the class names change, SAM 3 falls to chance and SnapHead's score is unchanged. End to end, with 20 labeled images, SNAP beats a SAM 3 oracle tuned on the evaluation labels on five microscopy projects (0.484 against 0.441 F1), and run unchanged on five held-out datasets, it beats SAM 3 as shipped on four. Our results suggest that frozen foundation features already encode the class boundaries a generic vocabulary misses, and that a project's own labels are enough to read them out.

title: YRC-Bench: Benchmarking Culturally Aware Machine Translation for Historical Heritage via Tri-Level Semantic Bridging
summary: Translating historical cultural heritage poses profound challenges for machine translation systems due to the acute semantic asymmetry across eras and cultures, where terse classical syntax frequently obscures domain-specific cultural knowledge. While Large Language Models have demonstrated remarkable prowess in generic translation benchmarks, they struggle to negotiate Culturally-Specific Items and diachronic shifts in domain-rich historical texts, such as Yellow River cultural records. To bridge this critical gap, we introduce YRC-Bench, the first human-curated, multi-parallel benchmark dedicated to historical heritage translation across Classical Chinese, Modern Chinese, and nine target foreign languages. YRC-Bench establishes a tri-level parallel corpus incorporating modern explanatory glosses as explicit semantic bridges and operationalizes translation strategies through paired conserved versus substituted CSI variants categorized by cultural translatability. Systematic evaluations of nine leading LLMs across bidirectional translation directions reveal that leveraging modern Chinese glosses - especially human-curated ones - dramatically elevates both lexical fidelity and semantic adequacy. Furthermore, multidimensional human preference audits by native experts unveil distinct cross-cultural preferences between Sinographic-tradition and non-Sinographic language groups.

title: Contrastive fine-tuning against stain and scanner bias improves robustness and downstream performance across pathology foundation models
summary: Histopathology foundation models achieve strong performance across diverse downstream tasks, yet their representations have been shown to encode scanner- and site-specific biases, creating generalization gaps and potentially limiting real-world utility. We introduce SPECTRA (Scanner and Pathology Embedding Contrastive Tuning for Robust Alignment), a model-agnostic contrastive learning post-training framework which explicitly encourages scanner- and stain-robust representations, to optimize performance and generalization on downstream applications. Using parameter-efficient LoRA adapters trained on matched multi-scanner and multi-stain whole-slide images sourced from the PLISM dataset, our method aligns spatially corresponding regions across acquisition conditions (scanner, stain), using other locations within each candidate condition as negatives. SPECTRA improved PathoROB robustness index, gene-expression prediction on HEST, slide-level classification AUC on CPTAC, and held-out PLISM retrieval for every model. Overall tile-level classification on THUNDER also improved, with exceptions for segmentation and calibration tasks. We open-source our training and evaluation codebases and release adapters and model weights for selected backbones.

title: onóna: Twin Embeddings with Tied Unembeddings
summary: Weight tying reduces the parameter cost of language models, but the usual tied output head is limited to a single softmax. We introduce onóna, a two-table parameterization that increases output expressiveness while preserving input-output weight sharing. The Transformer takes the average of two embedding tables as input, and the output head combines the softmax distributions defined by those same tables. A gate conditioned only on the current input token determines the mixture weight. Its values can be precomputed for inference, and the Transformer body remains unchanged. We evaluate onóna across Dense, Gated DeltaNet hybrid, mixture-of-experts, and Attention Residual architectures at 142M, 330M, and 1B scales. Under matched token budgets, onóna lowers final validation loss and external perplexity in 11 of 12 comparisons and raises the average accuracy over eight downstream tasks in 10 of 12. The one exception on loss is the 1B MoE model. The cost is one extra embedding table and one extra vocabulary projection.

title: A Privacy-Aware Deep Learning Benchmark for Facial Emotion Recognition
summary: Facial Expression Recognition (FER) traditionally relies on raw RGB images, introducing privacy risks, sensitivity to illumination variations, and susceptibility to identity-confounding visual shortcuts. As an alternative, this work proposes a lightweight, privacy-aware pipeline using exclusively geometric representations-facial landmarks (478 points) and blendshapes (52 coefficients, ARKit standard)-eliminating persistent raw video storage. Six neural architectures trained from scratch on fused CREMA-D and RAVDESS datasets were benchmarked against an ImageNet-pretrained ResNet50 baseline under a 5-fold subject-independent cross-validation protocol. Geometric models consistently outperformed the pixel baseline on unseen subjects with 12-124 times fewer parameters, while demonstrating superior robustness on subtle emotional expressions such as sadness. Ablation studies reveal that blendshapes capture the primary discriminative signal, while landmarks provide essential complementary spatial topology. These results demonstrate that compact geometric representations preserve affective semantics, eliminate downstream transfer learning dependency on visual backbones, and enable efficient, privacy-aware emotion recognition.

title: Large Language Models without QK-Normalization
summary: Query-Key Normalization (QK-Norm) is widely adopted in modern large language models to control the growth of attention logits and improve training stability. However, query and key norms are not merely sources of instability. The query norm controls the sharpness of the attention distribution, while the key norm determines how strongly a token attracts different queries. These norms therefore carry token-specific information about attention selectivity and token importance. By normalizing both, QK-Norm suppresses this information. This raises a natural question: can we control query-key representations without discarding their sensitivity to magnitude? To address this question, we propose QK-MAP, a Magnitude-Aware Projection for constructing queries and keys. Rather than removing magnitude through normalization, QK-MAP transforms the input representation using multiple learnable frequencies, so that changes in magnitude are encoded as bounded phase patterns. This allows magnitude to be represented through phase and direction rather than vector length alone. Its periodic features have a fixed norm while remaining sensitive to magnitude changes, separating magnitude encoding from norm growth. Multiple frequencies further help distinguish magnitudes and reduce periodic ambiguity. Experiments across model scales from 190M to 7B parameters show that QK-MAP achieves lower training and validation loss than both Standard attention and QK-Norm. Further analyses show that QK-MAP preserves sensitivity to input scale, assigns less attention to the first token, and produces stronger attention contrast for relevant evidence in synthetic long-context tests. These results demonstrate that query-key scale can be effectively controlled without sacrificing token-specific magnitude information.

title: Improving the Diffusability of Motion Tokenizer
comment: Accepted to NeurIPS 2026 (Spotlight). 26 pages, including appendix
summary: Latent diffusion models paired with a variational auto-encoder (VAE) tokenizer have shown promising performance for efficient text-driven human motion generation. However, motion latent diffusion suffers from a generation-reconstruction trade-off: simply increasing tokenizer capacity enhances reconstruction but fails to proportionally improve text-conditioned generation quality. We assume this trade-off stems from a spectral mismatch inside the VAE tokenizer: the encoder yields a latent space biased toward high frequencies, and the decoder introduces temporal artifacts. In this paper, we propose the Diffusable Motion Tokenizer (DiMoT) to improve the diffusability of the tokenizer, rather than scaling up the diffusion backbone. To improve text-conditioned optimization, Critic Spectral Adaptation (CSA) leverages a pretrained diffusion model as the critic to suppress high-frequency latent energy. To preserve motion dynamics, the Alpha-Flow Motion Decoder (AMD) performs generative decoding via average-velocity prediction, enabling efficient one-step decoding. Extensive experiments demonstrate that DiMoT achieves state-of-the-art performance across various challenging text-to-motion benchmarks, yielding superior motion fidelity and text-motion alignment. Project page: https://githubhgh.github.io/dimot/.

title: Global Context Guidance for Diffusion Large Language Models
summary: Diffusion large language models (LLMs) have recently emerged as a promising alternative to autoregressive LLMs, enabling parallel generation through iterative denoising. Recent guidance methods improve diffusion LLMs by introducing a weak model to guide the prediction of the base model during denoising. However, the influence of the weak model during denoising remains less clear, and computing its prediction requires an additional forward pass at each denoising step. We present in this paper an in-depth analysis of how diffusion LLMs use contextual information during denoising. Our analysis reveals that diffusion LLMs rely more heavily on local context while often underutilizing global context. Based on this observation, we introduce Global Context Guidance (GCG), a feature-space guidance method that enhances global-context utilization without constructing an explicit weak model. Extensive experiments on LLaDA-8B, Dream-7B, and LLaDA-1.5 across diverse benchmarks demonstrate that GCG consistently outperforms existing guidance methods, while incurring much lower inference overhead.

title: CXR-CMFA: A Cross-Modal Feature Aggregation Network for Chest X-Ray Pathology Classification
summary: Chest X-ray (CXR) interpretation remains challenging because subtle pathology can be obscured by overlapping anatomy, image-quality variation, and limited visual evidence in isolated radiographs. Although image-only deep learning models provide useful baselines, they discard the complementary diagnostic context available in radiology reports, while large vision-language models can be computationally expensive for practical deployment. This paper presents CXR-CMFA, a lightweight cross-modal feature aggregation network for binary CXR pathology classification. The proposed framework combines a dual-stream visual encoder, using EfficientNet-B0 for global anatomical representation and DenseNet-121 for local pathological detail, with a TF-IDF-MLP report encoder. Two fusion modules integrate these modalities: the Dual-Modal Spatial Attention Module (DMSAM) uses the report embedding to gate global and local visual features, and the Cross-Modal Gated Feature Fusion (CGFF) module learns per-instance weights for visual and textual contributions. Experiments on the MIMIC-CXR benchmark, using the provided train, validation, and test splits, show that CXR-CMFA achieves 93.45% accuracy, 99.88% precision, 91.8% recall, 95.7% F1-score, and 99.19% AUC on the held-out test set. The model produces only four false positives among 984 normal test cases, supporting its suitability for high-specificity screening workflows. An ablation study further demonstrates a 22.47 percentage-point AUC improvement over the global-image-only variant, confirming the value of adaptive cross-modal fusion. These results indicate that compact report-conditioned fusion can provide strong discriminative performance without relying on large pretrained language models.

title: AI in the Clinical Documentation Loop: Effects of LLM-Induced Note Bloat and Diagnostic Overcall on Downstream LLMs
summary: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used to process medical records for healthcare tasks such as clinical documentation. Because these tools also generate documentation, the relationship is now bidirectional: models both read from and write to the record. Understanding how LLMs behave when reading records that already contain LLM-authored content is therefore critical for their safe deployment. In this study, we examine how LLM-authored content in the medical record affects downstream LLMs that read the same record. We consider two types of LLM-induced artifacts: bloat, in which LLM-generated summaries accumulate in the record and change the length and provenance of its content over time; and distortion, in which LLMs subtly alter clinical findings rather than fabricating facts outright. As a case of distortion, we study diagnostic overcall (documenting an unconfirmed differential diagnosis in the record) and test whether it propagates to the reader LLM's output. Across seven reader models from four families, we find evidence of both effects. First, LLM-generated summary notes modestly but consistently degraded downstream hospital-course generation compared with copy-forward and templated text of matched length. Second, injected overcalls reappeared in downstream outputs at rates that varied by reader model, without detectable changes in standard quality metrics. These findings show the need to monitor AI-generated content in medical records and to account for it when those records are later processed by AI.

authors: Ronald L. P. D. de Jong
title: ATLAS: A Multi-Procedure Benchmark and Context-Aware Model for Surgical Anatomy Segmentation
summary: Recognizing anatomical structures during minimally invasive surgery (MIS) could support intraoperative navigation and improve patient safety, but progress is limited by small, single-procedure datasets and by segmentation methods developed for natural scenes. This work addresses both limitations through a new dataset and model. First, we introduce ATLAS-120k, a clip-level semantic segmentation dataset of 121,018 annotated frames from 100 surgical videos, covering 14 laparoscopic and robot-assisted procedures and 41 classes. Annotations were created with a pipeline that combines manual labeling, tracker-based propagation, and review by surgeons. Second, we propose ATLAS (Anatomy Recognition with Context Learning using Foundation Representations), a video semantic segmentation model for surgical anatomy recognition. ATLAS builds on in-domain foundation-model embeddings and adds context queries for the procedure and surgical phase, together with query propagation between frames for short-term memory. ATLAS outperforms state-of-the-art natural-image and in-domain foundation models in both segmentation accuracy and temporal consistency, achieving a Dice score of 0.70 with ViT-L while running in real time at 76.2 FPS. Ablations show that the context queries improve accuracy and that query propagation improves temporal consistency. ATLAS also generalizes well, matching a dedicated model zero-shot on CholecSeg8k and improving phase recognition on AutoLaparo over SurgeNet initialization. The model weights, dataset annotations, and annotation tool are publicly available at https://github.com/TimJaspers0801/ATLAS.

title: On the Geometric Bottlenecks of Cross-Lingual Knowledge Editing
summary: Transformer-based autoregressive multilingual language models (LMs) are often assumed to store factual knowledge in an interlingua: a language-agnostic latent space. If this assumption holds, a parameter update applied in a source language during knowledge editing should inherently propagate to its semantic equivalents in target languages. However, empirical benchmarks show that cross-lingual propagation of edits often degrades substantially, a degradation that prior work treats largely as an algorithmic symptom rather than a structural bottleneck. In this work, we investigate whether representational anisotropy creates a structural bottleneck for source-only associative-memory editing, and perform a geometric dissection of the cross-lingual propagation gap. Using associative memory-based "locate-then-edit" methods, including ROME, MEMIT, and AlphaEdit, as analytical frameworks, we derive a closed-form decomposition of this gap into key-space propagation, parallel residual mismatch, and orthogonal residual mismatch. Our empirical findings show that cross-lingual propagation is primarily bottlenecked by a large orthogonal residual component, indicating that source-language edits often fail to span the target-language update directions required for successful transfer. Furthermore, we show that post-hoc correction using only source-language residual statistics encounters a large residual-prediction barrier. Finally, we perform a structural realignment via a targeted contrastive alignment objective and find that it substantially improves key-space propagation and partially improves cross-lingual edit transfer, while leaving value-space mismatch as a remaining bottleneck.

title: RigidGS: Geometry-Aware Object Decoupling for Rigid-Body Interaction in 3D Gaussian Splatting
comment: 12 pages, 5 figures, 7 tables. Accepted at WACV 2027 (Applications Track). Project page: https://gyreyirisansah.github.io/rigidgs
summary: Interactive VR/MR applications demand photorealistic 3D representations that support real-time rendering and object-level manipulation. While 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) achieves high rendering quality, it represents scenes as unstructured, monolithic primitives. Existing object-aware 3DGS methods jointly optimize geometry and semantic states but suffer from two key failure modes: noisy foundation-model masks on complex geometry, and label-geometry coupling, in which co-optimized identity gradients mislabel boundary Gaussians. We introduce RigidGS, an end-to-end pipeline that decouples geometric learning from object identity. We propose a depth- and temporally-aware mask refinement module that addresses two complementary SAM2 failures: over-inclusion on thin structures and under-inclusion on multimodal-depth objects. We then determine object identities entirely upstream via COLMAP projection voting and freeze them during training, directing mask supervision solely toward geometric optimization. Refined masks alone substantially improve competing methods, yet a residual gap in label-geometry coupling persists that our fixed-identity design eliminates. RigidGS outperforms prior object-aware 3DGS methods on LLFF/NVOS, Mip-NeRF~360, and iNeRF360, improving segmentation and boundary IoU by 7.7 and 14.5 points on LLFF/NVOS. Finally, RigidGS enables real-time rigid-body manipulation on Meta Quest~2 without mesh extraction. Our code and project page are available at https://gyreyirisansah.github.io/rigidgs.

title: TransMem: Transition-Aware Retrieval for Evolving Personal Memory
summary: Long-term personalized agents are increasingly expected to answer queries over user histories in which preferences, goals, and constraints evolve across interleaved conversations. Existing retrieval-based and structured-memory systems can surface relevant facts, but often return isolated memory units that do not explain which earlier preference was refined, contradicted, or superseded by later evidence. We introduce TransMem, a transition-aware memory retrieval framework that stores preference updates as explicit retrieval units alongside ordinary factual memories. During memory construction, TransMem routes user interaction history into topic-structured memory graphs, detects shift events, and grounds them as transition records. At inference time, TransMem first retrieves factual anchors and then adaptively expands over transition records, producing a compact context of factual anchors and accepted transition records. Experiments on PersonaMem and PersonaBench across two Qwen backbones show that TransMem outperforms representative retrieval-based and structured-memory baselines. Controlled analyses further show that transition records and adaptive expansion contribute beyond factual anchoring, chronological expansion, flat transition retrieval, and fixed-hop traversal. These results suggest that preference-update records are useful retrieval units for long-term personalization.

title: Anatomy-Preserving Unpaired Medical Image Translation via Shared Latent Anchoring
summary: Unpaired medical image-to-image translation requires synthesizing target-modality images from source-modality images without aligned supervision. Existing methods learn a direct source-to-target mapping that entangles structure preservation and appearance generation within a single model, often distorting clinically meaningful anatomy in the translated output. We argue that these two objectives should be decoupled entirely: anatomical structure should be captured independently of generation, and the generator should operate only on a frozen structural representation. To this end, we propose a two-stage framework for unpaired medical image translation. In the first stage, we learn a shared structure space by training a structure encoder-decoder on source images, target images, and structural masks jointly, using mask reconstruction to anchor the latent space to modality-agnostic anatomy. For source images without mask annotations, a target-domain memory bank provides soft structural supervision via prototype retrieval. In the second stage, a conditional flow model learns to render target-domain appearance under fixed structural conditions. This ensures the generator inherits target appearance statistics and can focus entirely on structural conditioning rather than learning appearance from scratch. We validate our framework on OCT-to-OCTA synthesis and brain MR-to-CT translation. Our method outperforms all unpaired baselines on both tasks and, despite requiring no paired supervision, also surpasses paired baselines, improving PSNR by up to 11.2% and SSIM by up to 26.4% on OCT-to-OCTA, and achieving consistent gains across whole-image, soft-tissue, and bone regions on MR-to-CT. The project repository is available on GitHub.

title: Behavioral Evaluation of Large Language Models Under Cognitive Biases in HAZOP Studies
comment: 8 pages, 1 figure, 3 tables. Submitted to IFAC for possible publication. Supplementary material available at https://github.com/ViniMelloeMuller/psyhazop-supplementary-material
summary: Hazard and Operability (HAZOP) studies safeguard industrial processes against catastrophic accidents. Large language models (LLMs) increasingly assist HAZOP drafting, yet evaluations rely on lexical overlap. Because LLMs internalize human heuristics, prompts may trigger biased judgments. Whether frontier LLMs withstand cognitive perturbations in safety-critical workflows remains unknown. Here we show across 420 trials that three frontier LLMs resisted 96.8% of cognitive manipulations, rendering overall susceptibility statistically inconclusive. Contrary to assumed broad fragility, models rejected confirmation and availability cues. However, safety-critical risk downgrades emerged under low anchors and gain frames. Thus, automated hazard analysis requires disciplined human-in-the-loop validation.

title: From Weapons to Events: Evaluating Evidential Support in Multimodal AI for Policing
comment: 34 pages, 2 figures, 4 tables; appendices include annotation guidelines, prompt templates and a datasheet
summary: Computer vision (CV) for policing has centred on recognising objects such as seized weapons, while body-worn video (BWV) is still reviewed by people, with existing AI tools using only its audio. Multimodal video AI could make BWV review faster and cheaper. At the object level, we present the KnifeHunter dataset, developed with UK law enforcement, with over 25,000 images of 543 knife classes and a protocol reflecting investigative conditions, and KHNet, a retrieval architecture fusing local and global features, which with about 125,000 distractor images attains 85.7% and 63.4% mean Average Precision (mAP) on the medium and hard protocols. At the event level, we present an evaluation protocol for video understanding pipelines, which describe a video as events and a transcript, that scores transcription, speaker attribution, event detection, temporal localisation and unsupported events. Whether each event is supported by the recording is labelled by a judge validated against blinded human labels. We apply it to complete pipelines, three 2026 omni-modal models and our hybrid NarrativeBridge-PAL-GPT-5 pipeline, on UKBWV-27, a pilot stress-test set of 27 publicly released UK BWV recordings (118 minutes). On this set the hybrid pipeline leads on five of six measures, yet it leaves 13.6% of predicted events unsupported and misattributes 27.7% of utterances, and every pipeline degrades on recordings from edited releases, long recordings and noisy audio. We propose readiness levels separating assistive tasks from those requiring verification of every output.

title: Evaluating Physically Grounded Procedural Reasoning in VLMs through Real-World Execution: Crochet as a Testbed
summary: Vision-Language Models (VLMs) can generate procedures that look convincing on paper, but do they work in practice? In this paper, we propose crochet as an ideal testbed for physically grounded procedural reasoning in VLMs. Crochet cannot be reliably simulated or automated: the only way to know what a pattern produces is to make it by hand, yet verification is tangible and cheap, requiring nothing but a hook and a ball of yarn. We introduce FoundationChain, a deceptively simple test of procedural reasoning: given an image of a basic crochet object, can VLMs infer how it was made and generate a pattern that produces the same result? We crochet 40 patterns generated by four VLMs by hand. Even at this scale, physical execution not only reveals failures that automated proxies cannot detect, but also enables a more precise diagnosis of their causes and consequences: while models write fluent, convincing patterns, only four are free of errors, and our analysis exposes deficiencies in visual, geometric and procedural reasoning.

title: Beyond Frame-Level Accuracy: Analyzing Video-Level Stability in Transformer-Based Deepfake Forensics
comment: Paper submitted to international journal of intelligent systems, Wiley publishers, accepted version of open-access paper
summary: Deepfake videos generated by advanced generative models pose serious threats to digital security, misinformation control, and media forensics. Although numerous detection methods have been proposed, their reported performances are often based on heterogeneous preprocessing pipelines, inconsistent data splits, and model-specific training protocols, hindering fair architectural comparison. This work presents a controlled and reproducible comparative study of convolutional neural networks (ResNet-18 and EfficientNet-B0) and a transformer-based architecture (ViT-B/16) within a unified, face-centric deepfake detection framework. All models are trained using identical preprocessing, augmentation, optimization settings, and data splits on Celeb-DF v2 and FaceForensics++, and results are validated across three independent random seeds with bootstrapped confidence intervals. Experimental results show that while CNN-based models perform competitively at the frame level, their performance degrades after video-level aggregation. In contrast, ViT-B/16 demonstrates more stable video-level performance, achieving 92.8\% [95\% CI: 91.7--94.0] video-level accuracy and an AUC of 0.950 [95\% CI: 0.934--0.964] on Celeb-DF v2 (3-seed bootstrapped). Cross-dataset evaluation across the same three random seeds reveals a large, asymmetric generalization gap (AUC 0.79 FF++$\rightarrow$Celeb-DF vs. 0.64 Celeb-DF$\rightarrow$FF++), indicating that in-domain video-level stability does not transfer to unseen manipulation domains. These findings indicate that global self-attention improves robustness and video-level stability for deepfake detection within a given data domain, while highlighting the need for further work on cross-domain generalization.

title: Cascading Circle Loss: Order-Preserving Contrastive Learning for Graded Legal Retrieval
summary: This paper introduces Cascading Circle Loss (CasCL), a contrastive learning framework for legal retrieval tasks with graded relevance. CasCL combines an InfoNCE objective for positive-negative separation with a cascade of ranking boundaries that model ordered relevance levels between queries and legal clauses. The framework also includes a negative-aware self-paced optimization mechanism and a relevance gain weighting strategy to improve ranking quality. Experiments on legal passage retrieval benchmarks show that CasCL consistently outperforms existing methods, including InfoNCE, Circle Loss, MNRL and Margin MSE, across both binary retrieval and graded ranking metrics.

title: STAIRS: Staging the Inverse Problem via Admissible-Support Scheduling for Unrolled MRI Reconstruction
summary: Accelerated magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) forms images from incomplete Fourier measurements, shifting acquisition burden to computational reconstruction. Deep unrolled networks interleave learned regularization and data consistency, yet typically estimate the full unmeasured spectrum at every cascade. We propose STAIRS (Staging the Inverse Problem via Admissible-Support Scheduling), which projects intermediate reconstructions onto nested Fourier supports that expand to the full spectrum and conditions each update on its support transition. Conditional increments of a regularized log-determinant score of training covariance define a normalized spectral coordinate, accounting for dependencies between newly and previously admitted frequencies. Dyadic targets allocate larger coordinate increments to earlier cascades and are mapped to fixed supports before training, enabling coarse-to-fine reconstruction with unchanged sampling masks and data consistency. On fastMRI and Stanford2D, STAIRS improves matched Transformer (HUMUSNet) and convolutional (NAFNet) backbones in single- and multi-coil reconstruction, including radiologist-annotated pathology regions. It also outperforms predictor-based progression with lower parameter overhead and inference latency. Stage-wise analysis shows repeated error correction by projection and lower intermediate reconstruction errors than the backbones alone throughout support expansion. Ablations favor dyadic allocation over uniform expansion for square and line-band supports and over manual front-loading for square windows. Support projection alone improves reconstruction, and transition conditioning strengthens the gain. Cross-dataset evaluation shows improvements for both backbones in both directions. Support allocation thus complements regularizer design in unrolled MRI reconstruction.

title: Adapting Large Language Models via Multi-Task Learning for Mental Health Problem, Emotion, and Sentiment Detection
summary: This study investigates sequential multi-task learning using Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning (PEFT), LoRA, and 4-bit quantization on Llama 3.1 8B Instruct for mental health problem detection, emotion detection, and sentiment analysis. Using 4,243 English social media posts, it compares two task sequences and demonstrates that task ordering significantly affects knowledge transfer and task interference. The MHP-first sequence achieves the best mental health problem detection (Micro-F1: 0.7624), while the Emotion-first sequence performs better in emotion (F1: 0.6052) and sentiment analysis (F1: 0.9459). A Joint-MTL baseline further highlights the challenges of simultaneous learning, including task interference and generative format collapse. Overall, the findings demonstrate the effectiveness of sequential PEFT for mental health NLP while showing that task order is critical to balancing performance across related tasks. The integration of LoRA and 4-bit quantization also reduces computational and memory requirements, supporting the adaptation of large language models in resource-constrained environments.

title: Domain Generalization for Style-Debiased Object Detection via Label-Consistent Training across Multiple Styles
summary: Domain generalization (DG) for object detection aims to improve model performance on unseen target domains. Existing detectors, however, suffer substantial degradation on visually distinct unseen domains, as models confined to limited training styles tend to overfit superficial statistical cues rather than object-level semantics. Motivated by human perception, which attends primarily to semantically relevant features while ignoring irrelevant style cues, we propose Origin-Anchored Multi-Style Consistency (OAMSC), a source-only framework that couples multi-style data synthesis with cross-style consistency learning to suppress style-sensitive shortcut learning. For data preparation, we leverage off-the-shelf diffusion models to expand the source datasets into 20 distinct styles, with all generated images manually verified to ensure that object instances and annotations remain consistent across style variants. During training, we impose Origin-anchored consistency constraints at scene and object levels to reinforce the learning of domain-stable features while suppressing the influence of style-sensitive cues. Extensive experiments and ablation studies on multiple challenging DG benchmarks demonstrate the consistent effectiveness and strong generalization performance of OAMSC across diverse domain shifts. Notably, our approach applies to both one-stage and two-stage detectors, while its data-centric design is complementary in principle to other DG methods. The training code and two style-transfer datasets constructed for the experiments, comprising approximately 180K images in total, are publicly available on GitHub.

title: Enhancing Mathematical Reasoning in Turkish Large Language Models with Search-Based Inference and Model Merging
summary: We improve Turkish mathematical reasoning in Large Language Models by combining LoRA fine-tuning, weight-space model merging, and search-based inference. Using Turkish-Llama 8B-DPO with Turkish translations of MetaMath, NuminaMath, and TigerLab, we find data quality beats scale (Mix-30k best among fine-tuned; large MetaMath underperforms). Linear merging delivers the largest gains (GSM8K up to 0.63), while Ties is modest and Breadcrumbs/Slerp degrade. Search with MCTS and Tree of Thoughts improves mean LLM-judge scores for reasoning quality on a 0-100 scale. Limitations include machine translation, limited scale, and search stochasticity.

title: DAC-MACE: Context-Conditioned Expert Routing for Compact Scene Coordinate Regression in Camera Relocalization
comment: 10 pages, 6 figures. Submitted to IEEE Sensors Journal
summary: A camera becomes an absolute pose sensor when its images can be relocalized against a prebuilt map of the scene. On mobile robots and augmented-reality devices, that map must be small and quick to build. Scene coordinate regression (SCR) stores the scene in a compact network that predicts a 3D coordinate for every pixel, and mixture-of-experts (MoE) variants extend its capacity to larger outdoor scenes. In existing MoE-based SCR, however, the router assigns each pixel to an expert from the same local descriptor that the experts regress from, so repeated facades and windows at different locations receive similar routing inputs. We present DAC-MACE, which conditions soft expert routing on recalibrated and contextualized features. A residual context adapter (RCA) reweights the channels and locations of frozen encoder features, a global context encoder (GCE) mixes them with multi-scale self-attention, and an image-level pooled descriptor is added to the router input. A dual-threshold RANSAC--Levenberg--Marquardt estimator recovers the pose. On Cambridge Landmarks, DAC-MACE attains a mean per-scene median translation error of 13.0 cm over three seeds, the lowest among the RGB-only SCR methods compared (GLACE 13.6 cm, MACE 14.4 cm), and reduces the error on the largest scene from 24 to 19 cm relative to MACE. In a cumulative study, the MoE head, GCE, RCA, and the dual-threshold estimator lower the mean error from 17.0 cm to 14.4, 14.0, 13.6, and 13.0 cm. On 7-Scenes, adding GCE to a single ACE head raises Recall@(5 cm, 5$^\circ$) from 86.56% to 87.60%.

title: Evaluating Jev on Arabic: Comparing Decision Models and LLMs Across Arabic Tasks and Dialects
summary: How does Jev compare with other systems on Arabic tasks, and how does its performance change between Modern Standard Arabic (MSA) and dialects? We evaluate 67 systems, including 47 decision models and 20 large language models (LLMs), on 43 tasks across 9 task families using a shared zero-shot protocol. The Arabic-focused frozen suite includes English controls in three parallel resources, which we also remove in a separate descriptive comparison. Jev 1.14.0 achieves a mean task-primary metric of 69.24 on a scale multiplied by 100, compared with 68.77 for Jev 1.13.0 and 71.81 for Gemma-4-31B, the highest-scoring system on this aggregate. Removing the recorded English controls, repeated cross-task items or both leaves the full system order unchanged. Relative performance and gains between Jev versions vary across task families. In content-matched comparisons within Jev 1.14.0, pooled dialect-minus-MSA accuracy gaps range from -7.94 to -0.35 percentage points across four datasets; dialect-specific results show larger variation, and SIB-200's source-clustered interval includes zero. Paired contrasts with Jev 1.13.0, Gemma-4-31B and Jais-2-8B show a larger Palestinian banking penalty for Jev 1.14.0 than for either LLM under simultaneous uncertainty; the other gap contrasts remain inconclusive. These descriptive findings show why aggregate scores should be read alongside task-family results, coverage and matched language comparisons. They do not establish a general model ranking for dialect robustness or explain the causes of the observed gaps.

title: Uncertainty, Not Concealment: A Mechanistic Reappraisal of Sycophancy in Vision-Language Models
comment: Accepted to the NeurIPS 2026 Med-Reasoner Workshop
summary: Vision-language models (VLMs) in medical retrieval-augmented generation must be able to say when a retrieved report contradicts the X-ray, so understanding whether they can detect such conflicts is important for safe deployment. The sycophancy mask hypothesis holds that these models internally detect conflicts but refuse to report them, concealing a detected contradiction. We introduce a three-part diagnostic that separates concealment from uncertainty: representation probing, activation steering, and two-way forced choice. Across four instruction-tuned VLMs on chest X-rays, we confirm behavioral suppression of contradiction and find that a linear probe separates matched from mismatched inputs, beyond what a simple CLIP model achieves. Steering the learned conflict direction never elicits contradiction, and forcing a binary choice does not recover one; instead, cross-modal attention to the image drops on mismatched pairs. We conclude that these models fail to contradict because the mismatch registers as hedged, gated uncertainty rather than concealed knowledge, calling for re-grounding and uncertainty surfacing. Code is available at https://github.com/mohamed-eldagla/Uncertainty-Not-Concealment/.

title: Simple Test-Time Refinement for Plot-to-Code Generation via Visual-Code Diagnostics
summary: Plot-to-code generation has been greatly advanced by recent multimodal large language models (MLLMs). However, existing studies mainly focus on one-pass generation or iterative sampling guided by verifier-based filtering, which does not align with the typical human programming workflow of generate first, then iteratively error-location and fix. This naturally motivates a test-time refinement paradigm for plot-to-code generation. In this work, we present the first study on plot-to-code generation via iterative test-time refinement. We propose a Visual-Code Diagnostics framework that enables refinement through visual feedback from source code. Specifically, we first categorize generation errors into four coarse-grained types, and then train lightweight discriminators to recognize and localize these errors based on the rendered visual outputs and corresponding code. Unlike traditional compiler- or debugger-based verification, our approach performs iterative refinement guided by one diagnostics system, enabling more effective semantic and visual correction during test time. Extensive experiments demonstrate that our method consistently improves generation quality across diverse generators and significantly outperforms strong test-time scaling baselines.

title: AI-Driven Repair of Missing Automotive Components
summary: Due to supply constraints, replacing damaged automotive components can be expensive and time-consuming, while replacing the entire component can be wasteful when much of it remains usable. This paper presents a pipeline to investigate whether missing geometry can be reconstructed as a repair patch using paired observations of the intact models and synthetically damaged components. Noise-free color, depth, and silhouette images were produced using the camera viewpoints. Depth differences were then used to identify the potential missing regions, while multi-view voxel reconstruction was used to estimate the missing portion. A pretrained DINOv2 model was also added to validate missing candidates and determine whether pretrained visual features could improve reconstruction. We tested the pipeline on 20 automotive CAD models, each with a synthetically removed portion. Each model was tested under four different conditions using two reconstruction methods for a total of 160 trials. The predictions were compared with the missing geometry of the unchanged ground-truth using predefined thresholds of the voxel intersection-over-union over 0.85 and the absolute relative volume error less than 15%. Of the 160 experimental trials, 109 of them satisfied both thresholds. Geometry-only reconstruction passed 16 of 20 components with eight views but only 10 of 20 with four adjacent views. Further analysis showed that 24 out of the 37 failed reconstructions could be categorized as unsuccessful because extra material was incorrectly added to areas that should have been empty. The implementation of DINOv2 into the pipeline did not improve the overall reconstruction accuracy and made prediction generation slower. For 13 verified tests, printing only the repaired sections instead of the entire parts reduced filament use by 93.08% and printing time by 89.39% based on the median results.

title: MultiTurnRoute: A Platform for Building and Evaluating Multi-Turn LLM Routers
summary: In a multi-turn conversation, the choice of language model at one turn can affect which model should answer the next. The selected model's reply shapes the context for the next query, and its cached prompt prefix can reduce the cost of using that model again. We introduce MultiTurnRoute, a platform for building and evaluating multi-turn LLM routers. A shared interface gives built-in and user-defined routers the current query, dialogue history, and an estimate of each model's reusable prefix length. Our routing algorithm, Chain-of-Route (CoR), uses a learned gate over recent and recurrent dialogue history to predict response quality and estimates cost from each model's reusable prefix. MultiTurnRoute Arena ranks routers on recorded conversations and compares session quality and cost in interactive runs where a simulated user responds to each reply. On a benchmark drawn from WildChat and LMSYS-Chat-1M with per-turn quality annotations for five LLMs, CoR reduces the normalized cost required to match the strongest model's quality by up to 20.3% relative to the strongest routing baseline, while matching or improving peak response quality.

title: LoCo: Selective Local Competition for Discriminative Open-Vocabulary Multi-Label Recognition
comment: The paper is accepted by NeurIPS 2026
summary: Open-Vocabulary Multi-Label Recognition (OV-MLR) aims to identify all queried semantic concepts present in an image. Existing methods mainly improve global image-text matching or text-side representations, leaving local prediction largely under-explored. In this paper, we revisit local prediction and reveal that it can serve as a strong discriminative branch once two properties are properly handled: spatial consistency of local visual features and compatibility-aware local competition. This perspective is motivated by local semantic sparsity: each image region is related to only a small subset of queried concepts, while compatible concepts of different granularities or types may still coexist locally. We instantiate this perspective with LoCo, a selective Local Competition framework for OV-MLR. LoCo adopts a spatially consistent visual encoder to reduce local feature entanglement, and introduces Selective Softmax to impose competition only among locally incompatible categories while preserving compatible responses. Multi-scale inference further improves local prediction at different scales. LoCo can also be ensembled with an existing global predictor to provide complementary image-level context. Experiments on four multi-label benchmarks show that standalone LoCo improves average F1-score and mAP over TagCLIP by 3.4% and 3.8%, respectively. LoCo + DualPrompt achieves the highest averages among the compared methods, with gains of 4.8% and 5.2% over TagCLIP. Our results suggest that local semantic sparsity offers a useful basis for developing more discriminative open-vocabulary multi-label recognition methods. The code is available at https://github.com/lee-plus-plus/LoCo.

title: KeyASRBench: Measuring Whole-Phrase Keyword Preservation in Real-World ASR
comment: 8 pages, 3 figures, 4 tables. Bilingual ASR evaluation with a 10-hour model-conditioned challenge set and a disjoint 30-minute model-blind control
summary: Public automatic speech recognition (ASR) benchmarks increasingly report low sequence error rates, yet production systems still use hotword lists, contextual biasing, retrieval, and post-correction. This motivates a complementary question: does a transcript preserve selected names, products, technical terms, versions, and relational phrases? We present KeyASRBench, a bilingual pilot that operationalizes occurrence-based Keyword Error Rate (KER) over frozen whole-phrase annotations. The 10-hour model-conditioned challenge set contains 1,501 Chinese and English clips with 4,723 keyword occurrences. Across five locally inferred checkpoints and two official API systems, language-specific MER/WER ranges from 5.31% to 12.91%, while KER ranges from 13.61% to 33.81%. A disjoint 30-minute model-blind control yields KER of 10.65%-27.31%. The control confirms that selected-phrase errors extend beyond challenge-set selection.

title: TimeTraveler: Temporal Strategy Planning with Time Dictionary for Streaming Video Understanding
comment: Accepted at NeurIPS 2026. Project page: https://geppa.github.io/TimeTraveler
summary: Streaming video understanding (SVU) requires models to answer user queries over continuously evolving video streams. Unlike offline video QA, SVU must handle queries whose evidence may lie in the past, appear in the current scene, or emerge only after future observations. Existing streaming video systems often rely on compact visual memories or fixed evidence-access schemes, which can lose fine-grained details and fail to adapt the answering process to the temporal intent of each query. In this paper, we propose TimeTraveler, a streaming VQA framework that performs temporal strategy planning with a Time Dictionary. Inspired by the need to search across different temporal regions of a stream, TimeTraveler stores each observed moment as a timestamp-indexed structured caption and uses this dictionary as an explicit source of queryable evidence. Given a query, TimeTraveler determines whether to recall past evidence, read the present context, or wait for future observations, and then applies a strategy-specific evidence acquisition process. Comparative experiments on streaming video QA benchmarks show that TimeTraveler improves streaming question answering by preserving fine-grained temporal evidence and selecting the appropriate temporal strategy for each query. The project page is available at https://geppa.github.io/TimeTraveler.

title: SCorPion: A Strategic, Controllable and Personified Conversational Companion
summary: Fixed prompt-based language models face challenges in open-domain conversations, where versatile topics require different expert advice or demonstrations to maximize their universal performance. Motivated by the dynamic prompt studies in language generation, we extract different chatting strategies from varied forms of text corpus, which steer the language model to different styles based on human principles. We design and deploy a conversational companion called SCorPion, which uses GraphRAG to extract and summarize the knowledge graph globally, yield community-summarized strategies, and produce query-focused optimal strategies. SCorPion has strategic thinking, yields personified and stylized responses, and can be controlled by explicit factors. Code and further results can be found in https://bachozean.github.io/scorpion-page/.

title: MaRiO: Multi-agent Collaborative Reasoning via Shared Observations in MLLMs
comment: Accepted to the NeurIPS 2026 Evaluations & Datasets Track (poster). First two authors contributed equally
summary: Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) show strong visual perception capabilities, but existing evaluations largely focus on single-view or multi-view settings with shared camera parameters, leaving the challenge of multi-agent collaborative scenarios underexplored. In such settings, multiple agents observe a shared environment from independent viewpoints, and reliable decisions require reasoning across these independent observations of the same environment. To study this problem, we introduce MaRiO, a benchmark for evaluating multi-agent collaborative reasoning, and evaluate 23 state-of-the-art MLLMs on it. Our analysis reveals three key findings: (1) tasks governed by static perception are generally easier than tasks that require transformational event sequences; (2) most models struggle to resolve cross-agent correspondences, with errors increasing with scene complexity; and (3) models show limited ability to leverage geometric cues present in the scene. As an initial step toward addressing these challenges, we explore geometry-guided synthetic view augmentation that generates intermediate transition frames between agent observations, providing auxiliary spatial context that improves performance in certain categories. Overall, our results highlight that multi-agent collaborative reasoning remains an open challenge and an important direction for multimodal embodied systems. The code is available on the project page: https://omarftt.github.io/MaRiO-page/.

title: Pole or Vector? Encoders Capture Bangla Compound Verbs, but LLMs Read Them Literally
summary: In Bangla, a main verb is often followed by one of a small set of vector verbs. These verbs lose their own meaning and add a shade of meaning instead, such as completion. For example, likhe phello means that someone finished writing, not that they wrote and threw something. The same two verbs can also describe two separate events, so only the context shows which meaning is meant. This makes compound verbs a hard test of how language models handle multiword expressions. We present BanglaCV-Probe, a benchmark of 17 vector verbs with 1,044 minimal pairs, 204 entailment items and 197 pairs of correct and incorrect combinations, all checked by native speakers. We test 26 models (encoders, LLMs and translation systems) on four skills: telling the two meanings apart internally, understanding what a vector adds, preferring correct combinations and keeping the vector's meaning in translation. Probes on five encoders tell the two meanings apart and still reach up to 93% accuracy when trained on pairs without surface cues. Prompted models rarely use this knowledge. Entailment accuracy stays between 59% and 81%. Several LLMs answer Yes or No to almost every item, and nine of ten models miss that someone who ate up the rice left none. Most instruction-tuned LLMs translate vectors literally in 15-20% of vector sentences and in up to 55% for mora (die). On correct combinations, a small Bangla-only model (88%) matches BLOOM-7B1 (87%) and both beat Qwen2.5-7B (74%). Data and code: https://github.com/ashuvo25/Pole_OR_Vector

title: PoseBench: Probing Pose Awareness in Visual Foundation Models
summary: Pose awareness characterizes the extent to which a learned feature space aligns with the underlying object-pose manifold, such that observations with similar poses exhibit greater feature similarity than those with increasingly different poses. While such structure is desirable for pose-sensitive 3D vision tasks, visual foundation models pre-trained on individual 2D images typically lack explicit 3D or pose supervision. This raises a fundamental question: Do 2D visual foundation models exhibit pose awareness after large-scale pretraining? To answer this question, we introduce PoseBench, a systematic benchmark to probe pose awareness in pretrained visual features. Our evaluation follows a progressive design: held-out rendered views probe intrinsic pose-aware structure under controlled conditions, while real-image queries evaluate how robustly this structure remains accessible under real-world variations. We further introduce pose-graph-based refinement as a complementary probe of compatibility between feature neighborhoods and the underlying pose manifold. Across 31 publicly available checkpoints from 10 pretraining families, PoseBench reveals that pose awareness is an implicit but non-uniform property of 2D visual foundation models, and consistent gains from pose-graph refinement suggest that feature spaces retain structure compatible with the underlying pose manifold. PoseBench therefore provides a systematic basis for understanding and selecting pretrained features for pose-sensitive 3D vision tasks.

title: DeepFinance: Can AI Diligence a $100MM Deal?
summary: Existing evaluations of AI models on high-finance work focus on retrieving answers from financial documents and producing numerically correct outputs. Real private equity (PE) and investment banking (IB) work also depends on choosing between conflicting sources, making sound assumptions, and keeping every step auditable. We introduce DeepFinance, an ultra long-horizon benchmark of 21 end-to-end PE and IB tasks that take a human professional an average of 27.1 hours. Each task pairs a request with a data room averaging 19 files and is graded against an average of 84 expert-written rubric criteria covering output, workflow, and judgment. We evaluate 22 model configurations, each in its native agent harness. The best configuration, GPT-6 Astra with max reasoning, satisfies 57.6% of rubric criteria, and the top four configurations are not statistically distinguishable. Frontier models often calculate correctly from the wrong inputs and find decision-relevant evidence without acting on it.

title: Guided Co-Attention with Adaptive Gating for Multimodal Medical Data Fusion
summary: Multimodal fusion requires not only exchanging information across modalities but also determining which representations should participate in the interaction and how complementary cross-modal views should be combined. We introduce Guided Co-Attention with Adaptive Gating, a fusion framework that integrates token-wise guidance, bidirectional cross-attention, and sample-specific fusion. The proposed method constructs two directional representations: an image-conditioned text representation, obtained by allowing textual tokens to query visual features, and a text-conditioned image representation formed in the reverse direction. Token-wise guidance modulates the representations before cross-attention, while an adaptive gate learns the relative contribution of the two resulting directional representations for each sample. We evaluate the approach using paired chest radiographs and radiology reports as an image-text test bed for binary (normal vs. abnormal) classification. The two cross-attention directions exhibit distinct performance characteristics, demonstrating that reversing the query and source modalities does not produce interchangeable representations. Ablation experiments further show that bidirectional interaction, adaptive gating, and token guidance provide complementary benefits. The proposed model achieves 96.05% accuracy, 96.10% F1-score, 98.37% AUC, 95.60% Sens@95Spec, and 96.51% Spec@95Sens, yielding the highest mean performance across all evaluated metrics. These findings support explicitly modeling interaction direction, token relevance, and sample-dependent integration when constructing multimodal representations.

title: Gendered Misclassification from Surname-Based Race Imputation
summary: Researchers increasingly estimate political behavior based on race and gender from voter files, where race is imputed from surnames and geography. This only works where surnames suggest group membership, an assumption violated where surnames follow norms around marriage.
